title: When Economic Statecraft Stops Biting
hook: Tariffs and export controls are the two big levers of economic security policy. Both have a habit of losing force the longer they stay pulled.

title: Checks and Balances
hook: Separating power isn't enough — each branch also gets tools to limit the others, so power keeps power in check.

title: How a Legislature Undoes a Ballot Measure Voters Passed
hook: Missouri voters wrote abortion rights into their constitution in 2024. Lawmakers' answer wasn't to defy them — it was to put a second measure, with the same name, back on the ballot.

title: Populism
hook: Populism isn't a single program — it's a style that splits society into two camps: a virtuous 'people' against a corrupt 'elite,' with the populist speaking for the people.

title: The Welfare State
hook: Should the state guarantee a floor below which no one can fall? The welfare state is modern government's answer — and one of its biggest, most-debated commitments.

title: Nationalism & Identity
hook: The belief that the world divides naturally into 'nations,' each deserving its own state, is one of the most powerful political forces of the last two centuries — for unity and for conflict.

title: What Happens When a Country Defunds Its Public Broadcaster
hook: A year after the U.S. ended six decades of federal support for public media, the stations are still on air — but the mix of who pays for them, and which ones survive, has changed.

title: The Deepfake That Doesn't Have to Fool You Twice
hook: The most effective synthetic video isn't the most realistic one. It's the one that looks like something you already scroll past every day — a talk-show clip about yesterday's news.

title: Cynicism Is the Enemy of Reform
hook: Large majorities call the political system corrupt, across party lines. But some voters read the facts as outrageous and others as just how things work — and that split decides if anything changes.

title: How Out-of-Work Fishermen Aided the Revolution
hook: When Britain choked off New England's fisheries, thousands of skilled sailors lost their livelihoods overnight — and Washington gained the experienced seamen he badly needed.

title: Tariffs Aimed at Behavior, Not Just Trade
hook: A new round of U.S. tariffs was justified not as shielding domestic industry but as punishing countries for weak enforcement of forced-labor bans — trade policy used as a lever on someone else's laws.

title: Betting on What the President Will Say — From Inside the Room
hook: Prediction markets let anyone bet on politics. A White House staffer allegedly used his own front-row seat to Trump's speeches to place winning bets on Trump's own words.

title: What Federalism Is
hook: Some countries split authority between a national government and regional ones, each with powers the other can't simply override.

title: Media Trust Is Built Two Ways, Not One
hook: Most fixes for distrust in the press ask journalists to try harder. Research on Black communities in Minneapolis found the overlooked half is whether the community engages back.

title: Three Generations of Rights
hook: Human rights didn't all arrive at once. A useful map sorts them into three 'generations,' each born of a different era's struggles and demanding something different of the state.

title: Voting Against, Not For
hook: Many voters no longer back a candidate they admire — they vote to keep the other party out. That 'negative partisanship' can make even scandal forgivable.

title: Public Opinion & Polling
hook: What 'the people' think shapes what governments do — but measuring it is trickier than it looks, and a bad poll can mislead as easily as a good one informs.

title: How Official Statistics Earn Trust
hook: A government statistic carries weight only because of the process behind it. When a report skips the usual methodology and review, the number stops being evidence and becomes an argument.

title: A Visa Is Permission, Not a Right
hook: A visa does not entitle anyone to stay — it is a revocable permission to ask to be let in. That legal detail is why mass revocations can happen with a signature.

title: Readiness Is a Reserve You Spend
hook: A carrier's record 266-day deployment isn't a story about a weak military. It's a story about a budget nobody tracks: the finite reserve of crew rest and maintenance that every deployment draws down.

title: When the Law Carves Out an Exception for Belief
hook: Idaho parents can decline medical care for a sick child on religious grounds and be shielded from prosecution. That exemption is not ancient — a federal funding rule helped create it.

title: When Judges Step Aside
hook: A judge who might be biased is supposed to step aside. But on the U.S. Supreme Court, each justice decides that alone — and no one can overrule them.

title: Geofence Warrants & the Fourth Amendment
hook: Police can ask a tech company which phones were near a crime scene at a given hour — sweeping up everyone's location, not just a suspect's. In 2026 the Court said that's a 'search.'

title: When a Policy Reversal Becomes an Experiment
hook: A city banned needle exchange, then a court reinstated it. That accident handed researchers something rare in policy debate — a before-and-after test of the predicted harm.

title: Districts & Gerrymandering
hook: Where you draw the lines on a map can decide an election before a single vote is cast — which is exactly what gerrymandering exploits.

title: How Much Deference Does the Military Get?
hook: Courts scrutinize government classifications closely — except in the military, where judges have long deferred. A transgender service ban now tests where that deference stops.

title: War & Peace
hook: War is politics at its most extreme — organized violence between groups. Understanding why it happens, and how peace is kept, is central to the study of states.

title: 30x30 and the 'Paper Park' Problem
hook: The world pledged to protect 30% of the ocean by 2030. But a line on a map isn't protection — and much of what's been promised exists only on paper.

title: A Pattern Two Centuries Old: Backing the Opposition, Denying It Officially
hook: In 1805 a Venezuelan revolutionary asked Jefferson for help overthrowing Spanish rule. Jefferson denied involvement but quietly let him go — a pattern historians trace to 2026.

title: When Supreme Court Justices Rode the Circuit
hook: For over a century, sitting on the Supreme Court meant months on horseback hearing ordinary cases. Some reformers want a version of that back — and the reasons are revealing.

title: Making It Harder to Amend a Constitution — by Amending It First
hook: Some U.S. states are asking voters to approve a measure that would make future constitutional amendments harder to pass. It's direct democracy voting to limit direct democracy.

title: The Declaration of Independence
hook: It's remembered for 'life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness' — but most of the Declaration is a long list of grievances: a case that a government had broken faith with the governed.

title: Can Carbon Capture Solve Climate Change?
hook: What if we could keep burning fossil fuels and just vacuum the carbon back out? That promise is seductive, politically powerful — and, a major investigation argues, a mirage.

title: The Trillion-Dollar Budget No One Can Fully Trace
hook: Oversight needs a paper trail. ProPublica's look at U.S. defense spending finds the largest single pot of federal money is also the hardest to follow — and has never passed a full audit.

title: Interest Groups & Lobbying
hook: Between elections, organized groups press their case to government every day. Lobbying is how that pressure is applied — and it's both a feature and a worry of democracy.

title: How Extradition Works
hook: One country asking another to hand over a person is not a favor between friends — it runs on treaties and courts, and political goodwill is not the deciding vote.

title: States Are Writing AI Law First — and Federal Preemption Looms Over All of It
hook: With no comprehensive federal AI law yet, states have become the testing ground for regulating artificial intelligence. That leaves every state AI law exposed to a preemption fight.

title: Amending a Constitution
hook: A constitution has to last — but not freeze. Amendment rules let it change deliberately, usually demanding more agreement than an ordinary law.

title: Why Some Primaries Need a Second Round
hook: Win 34 percent of a crowded primary and in some states you're the nominee. In others, you go to a runoff — a rule that quietly reshapes which candidates survive.

title: When Legal Tools Switch Sides
hook: Doctrines aren't ideologies. Watch one Supreme Court term closely and you can see arguments long branded conservative being made by liberals, and vice versa.

title: Climate Opinion: Party Matters, But Not the Whole Story
hook: Party predicts how Americans feel about climate — but not the whole story: a young Republican may cheer solar panels and still reject a carbon tax.

title: When the Complaint Box Is the Only Oversight
hook: Give people in custody a form to file complaints and you can call it oversight. If nobody outside answers it, the next step isn't another form — it's a hunger strike.

title: When a 'Candidate' Texting You Is Actually a Bot
hook: Campaigns have always texted voters. Now some of those texts are AI-generated conversations trained to sound like the candidate — personalized, responsive, and not always clearly labeled.

title: Democracy vs Authoritarianism
hook: The deepest dividing line between regimes isn't left versus right — it's whether power can be lost. Can the people remove their rulers, or not?

title: When DNA Evidence Outlasts the Statute of Limitations
hook: A crime can go unprosecuted forever once its statute of limitations runs out — even if DNA later identifies a suspect. Massachusetts is one of the last states moving to close that gap.

title: A Strict Privacy Law Is Only as Strong as Its Enforcer
hook: A state can write the toughest data privacy law in the country and still see the data sold. Rights on paper need someone whose job is to notice when they're ignored.

title: Who Can Vote: Suffrage
hook: Democracy means rule by the people — but for most of history, 'the people' meant a narrow few. The story of suffrage is the slow widening of that circle.

title: When the Defendant Helps Decide What Evidence You Get
hook: A subpoena went to the city police, not the university. The university stepped in anyway to argue it was too broad — and won the right to help sort which files count.

title: When the Constitution Says Nothing Yet
hook: About 96,000 American children were born through IVF in 2023. The Supreme Court has barely addressed the technology — leaving state courts to invent the rules one dispute at a time.

title: Can You Predict a Ruling from Oral Argument?
hook: Courtroom folk wisdom says the side that gets grilled hardest is the side that loses. Someone finally checked the numbers — and the rule works, but barely better than a coin flip.

title: Civil Liberties Basics
hook: The freedoms that protect individuals from overreach by the state — like speech, belief, and a fair trial.

title: The Supreme Court of Japan
hook: Japan's top court has the power of constitutional review and almost never uses it: roughly ten laws struck down in eighty years, against 900-plus in the United States.

title: The Expert Who Shapes the Law
hook: Lawmakers regulating a product they do not understand call a scientist. Whether that scientist's travel was paid for by the industry is not a detail — it is the whole reliability question.

title: Three Kinds of Denial That Let Institutions Off the Hook
hook: Sociologist Stanley Cohen built a typology to explain how societies wave away state atrocities. It turns out to describe how any institution protects its own — one denial at a time.

title: It's Not That You Disagree — It's That I Think You're Wrong
hook: Polarization research usually assumes we dislike people who believe differently. Four studies suggest the sting comes from something narrower: believing the other person is factually mistaken.

title: The Federalist Papers
hook: To sell a skeptical public on the new Constitution, three founders wrote 85 newspaper essays under a single fake name. They're still the best guide to what it means.

title: When a Temporary Deployment Stops Being Temporary
hook: Emergency powers rarely end with an announcement. They end — or don't — through quiet extensions that never get the scrutiny the first decision did.

title: Gunshot Detection Tech
hook: Cities pay millions for microphones that promise to pinpoint gunfire and speed up police. The evidence that it actually works is surprisingly thin.

title: One Party, Both Chambers, Still No Bill
hook: Republicans hold the White House and both chambers of Congress. A signature voting bill is stuck anyway — a case study in why controlling government isn't the same as controlling the Senate.

title: How Many Jurors Make a Jury?
hook: Everyone pictures twelve. But in 1970 the Supreme Court called that number a 'historical accident' — and now it has agreed to look again.

title: The 1789 Law That Let the World Sue in U.S. Courts
hook: One sentence written by the first Congress quietly became America's main door for human rights lawsuits — and the Supreme Court has spent two decades narrowing it.

title: Trying Children as Adults
hook: Most legal systems treat young offenders differently — on the logic that a still-developing brain can change. So why are some children still tried in adult courts?

title: Trade & Protectionism
hook: Should a country trade freely with the world or shield its own industries? This single question has driven economic politics for centuries — and still does.

title: You Can Donate to the Government — You Can't Direct It
hook: Private money paying for a public building sounds like a bargain for taxpayers. Under U.S. law it mostly isn't allowed, because the power to decide what government spends belongs to Congress.

title: Two Doors to the Same Public Money
hook: A school Texas rejected as a charter got approved for taxpayer-funded vouchers months later. Same money, same state, different door — and a far lower bar.

title: Prices Vote: Economic Conditions and the Incumbent
hook: Voters rarely audit a governing record line by line. They ask a cruder question — is life more affordable than it was? — and that question moves elections more reliably than most policy debates.

title: Why Supreme Court Justices Have to Show Their Books
hook: Federal judges don't campaign for office or face voters — so how does the public keep tabs on their outside income, gifts, and travel? One tool: a legally required annual disclosure.

title: When the Agency Investigates Its Critics
hook: A man emailed criticism to the head of ICE. Agents later tracked him to his house, the airport and a hotel to ask about it. The knock itself is the constitutional problem.

title: Nuclear Weapons & Deterrence
hook: How do you stop a war you could never survive? The nuclear age answered with a chilling paradox: build weapons so terrible that no one dares use them.

title: What a Party Leader's Endorsement Is Actually Worth
hook: An endorsement is a signal, not an order. Primary voters keep the final say — and sometimes they use it against the person doing the endorsing.

title: Electoral vs Liberal Democracy
hook: Holding elections isn't the whole of democracy. Without rights, courts, and limits on the winner, voting alone can deliver an elected strongman.

title: When the Visiting Room Goes Video-Only
hook: A jail policy that looks like a small administrative choice — swap in-person visits for paid video calls — runs straight into what the research says keeps people from reoffending.

title: When New Maps Force a Second Primary
hook: Redraw a district map after candidates have already filed, and the calendar breaks: some Alabama voters had to nominate candidates twice in one year.

title: Who Gets to Regulate Betting on Elections?
hook: Wisconsin says you can't bet on an election you vote in — a law from 1849. The biggest prediction market calls that 'voter suppression.' Underneath sits a bigger question: which government decides?

title: Who Decides Where the Data Center Goes?
hook: A data center brings jobs and tax revenue — and noise, pollution, and higher power bills. Deciding whether to host one is a stress test for local democracy.

title: A Right With No Way to Sue Is Half a Right
hook: A prisoner's religious rights were violated and the harm was already done. The hard legal question was not whether it was wrong — it was whether he could recover anything at all.

title: When Two Candidates Agree, the Incumbent Usually Wins
hook: A challenger with nearly the same platform as the incumbent is asking voters to fire someone for no policy reason. That is the hardest race in politics — and it explains long legislative careers.

title: The Executive
hook: Laws don't enforce themselves. The executive is the branch that runs the state day to day — carrying out the law, commanding the bureaucracy, and acting in a crisis.

title: When Federal Law Means Different Things in Different States
hook: Nine federal appeals courts have read the same detention statute; seven say one thing and two say the opposite. Until the Supreme Court steps in, your rights depend on your address.

title: The Tragedy of the Commons
hook: When everyone shares a resource but no one owns it, each person's rational choice can add up to collective ruin. That trap explains a huge slice of environmental politics.

title: What Citizenship Is
hook: Citizenship is the formal bond between a person and a state — the status that turns a resident into a full member, with rights and duties to match.

title: Supreme Court Term Limits
hook: U.S. Supreme Court justices serve for life — unusual among democracies. A recurring reform would swap that for fixed terms. Why the idea keeps returning, and why it's so hard to enact.

title: How Opinion on Abortion Shifted After Dobbs
hook: When the Supreme Court returned abortion to the states in 2022, it didn't settle the debate — public opinion moved, with more Americans taking firm pro-access positions.

title: Monarchies, Republics & Regime Types
hook: Is the head of state a queen or a president? That old question — monarchy or republic — turns out to matter less than whether real power is elected and accountable.

title: Political Corruption
hook: Corruption is the abuse of entrusted power for private gain — and it quietly drains a society, eroding trust, fairness, and the resources meant for everyone.

title: Equality & Minority Rights
hook: Majority rule can become majority tyranny. Equality before the law and minority rights are how democracies stop the many from trampling the few.

title: Separation of Powers
hook: Split government into branches that make, enforce, and interpret the law — so no single part can do all three.

title: Proof of Citizenship to Vote
hook: Should you have to show a passport or birth certificate to register to vote? A fight in Congress over that single requirement reveals a deep tension in election design.

title: Political Parties & Party Systems
hook: Parties are how scattered voters become an organized choice. Whether a country has two big ones or a dozen shapes how its whole politics feels.

title: The Politics of Spectacle
hook: Bread and circuses, military parades, staged combat — leaders have always used spectacle to project power and bind people to a shared identity.

title: The Founder Who Became a Verb
hook: Elbridge Gerry signed the Declaration of Independence and served as vice president. He is remembered for a single map he signed in 1812 — and for the insult built from his name.

title: The History of Democracy
hook: Democracy isn't a permanent gift — it's a hard-won, on-and-off achievement that nearly vanished for two thousand years before its modern comeback.

title: Why a Big Resource Deal Doesn't Move the Price at the Pump
hook: Governments announce access to vast oil reserves and imply cheaper fuel. Oil in the ground and barrels on the market are separated by years of capital, and by a global price.

title: Who Gets to Decide What Goes on a Map
hook: Renaming a lake is not a matter of announcing it. In the U.S. a name normally climbs from town to county to state to a federal board — and stops entirely at the border.

title: The Office Whose Job Is Counting the Wrong Deaths
hook: Militaries do not automatically learn from killing civilians. Somebody has to be paid to investigate it, and that office can be closed as easily as it was opened.

title: Mail Ballot Grace Periods
hook: A ballot mailed on Election Day can still arrive days later. Should it count? States disagree — and in 2026 the Supreme Court sided with the states that say yes.

title: Nine Justices, Nine Styles
hook: One scholar coded 5,095 questions from a full Supreme Court term and found each justice interrogates lawyers in a signature way — a fingerprint of how they think about the law.

title: When Congress Overrides the Court
hook: A high court's ruling isn't always the last word. When judges interpret a statute, the legislature can often just rewrite the law — unless the decision rests on the constitution itself.

title: The Presumption of Regularity
hook: Courts normally start by assuming the government followed its own rules and told the truth. That default is quiet, load-bearing — and, judges are now saying out loud, forfeitable.

title: When Detention Conditions Become a Pressure Tactic
hook: Immigration detention is supposed to hold people while their case is decided — not persuade them to give up on it. Reporting from inside a Texas facility raises exactly that question.

title: Freedom of Information
hook: You can't hold power to account for what you can't see. Freedom of information laws pry open the workings of government so citizens can actually check it.

title: The Right to Understand Your Trial
hook: A trial you can't understand isn't a fair one — so the law promises defendants an interpreter. For speakers of rarer languages, that promise often goes unmet.

title: What Happens When a Senator's Seat Suddenly Opens Up
hook: When Sen. Lindsey Graham died in office in July 2026, South Carolina didn't call a snap election — it triggered a replacement process most voters never think about until it happens.

title: Who Decides Which Charities Get the Money?
hook: A donor-advised fund gives the tax break the day money goes in — but the money legally belongs to the sponsor, and the sponsor decides which charities may receive it.

title: The 'Widow's Mandate' and Inherited Political Power
hook: For most of a century, the fastest route for an American woman into Congress was her husband's death. That practice faded — but political inheritance never fully did.

title: Don't Trust the Name on the PAC
hook: The cheapest way to disguise who is talking to voters isn't a lie in the ad — it's a reassuring name on the group paying for it.

title: When 'AI Safety' Becomes Leverage
hook: Rules meant to protect the public can be turned into tools of control. One scholar argues some governments are repurposing 'AI safety' to pressure tech companies into line.

title: What Democracy Means
hook: Rule by the people: a system where political power ultimately traces back to citizens, usually through regular, free elections.

title: Why Ceasefires Break Down
hook: A ceasefire stops the shooting. It does not make peace. The difference — and the danger — lies in everything a quick deal leaves out.

title: The Pardon Isn't for Sale. The Advocacy Is.
hook: Paying for a presidential pardon outright would be a crime. Paying someone up to $5 million to get you in front of the president to ask for one? Perfectly legal — and a growing D.C. industry.

title: When a Lobby Starts Spending on Campaigns
hook: A lobbying group persuades officeholders. A campaign spender helps decide who the officeholders are. Crossing that line changes what a legislator is really being offered.

title: Self-Regulation and the Jurisdiction Gap
hook: When a private body governs an activity but sits outside every regulator's remit, weak rules stop being a flaw and start being a competitive advantage.

title: Public Goods & the State
hook: Some things markets struggle to provide — clean air, national defense, street lighting — because no one can be charged for them. That gap is a core reason states exist.

title: Ways to Participate
hook: Voting is the headline act of citizenship — but it's only one of many ways people shape politics, from joining a party to signing a petition or marching.

title: The Census Decides How Many Seats You Get
hook: A once-a-decade headcount sets each state's share of the House for ten years. A Florida challenge argues the count was done wrong — and shows why that is nearly impossible to fix afterward.

title: Sovereignty Among Nations
hook: Inside its borders a state is supreme — but in the world of states there's no higher ruler. That gap, called anarchy, shapes everything about international politics.

title: Can the President Fire the Heads of Independent Agencies?
hook: For 91 years, a 1935 precedent shielded independent agency heads from being fired at a president's will. In 2026 the Supreme Court swept most of that shield away.

title: Accountability & Oversight
hook: Power left unwatched drifts toward abuse. Accountability is the demand that officials answer for what they do — and oversight is the machinery that makes them.

title: How a Bill Becomes a Law
hook: An idea becomes binding law only after a journey: drafting, committee review, debate, votes, and final approval.

title: The People With No Opinion
hook: Researchers looking for antidemocratic attitudes kept finding something else: not opposition, not support, but a shrug. They argue the shrug is what makes erosion possible.

title: The First Amendment Clause That Stopped Doing Any Work
hook: The First Amendment names speech and the press separately — but the Court has folded the press clause into the speech clause, leaving journalists no rights an ordinary blogger lacks.

title: When Officials Sign an NDA
hook: A nondisclosure agreement is a private contract. When public officials sign one, the public loses its normal claim on what its own government is negotiating.

title: The Weak Point of Transparency Law: Silence
hook: A records law doesn't have to be repealed to stop working. An agency can simply not answer — and the only remedy left is a lawsuit most requesters can't afford.

title: The Calendar as a Legal Strategy
hook: Courts avoid changing election rules close to voting day. That gives a litigant a strange incentive: argue the other side sued too early, and the clock does the rest.

title: Taking Your Land for Someone Else's Server Farm
hook: The Fifth Amendment lets the government take private land for 'public use' with just compensation. Does a power line built to feed one company's data center count?

title: What a Court Minority Can Actually Force
hook: A losing bloc on a court can write a blistering dissent, or it can hold a procedural lever. Only one of those changes what the court does.

title: Presidential vs Parliamentary
hook: Two democracies can run on totally different wiring: in one, voters pick the leader directly; in the other, the legislature does — and that changes everything downstream.

title: The Legislature
hook: The branch that makes the law is also where a society argues out loud — the legislature turns competing interests into binding rules through debate and votes.

title: The Social Contract
hook: Why should anyone obey the state? The social contract answers: people trade some freedom for the security and order that only collective authority can provide.

title: Local Officials Run the Election; Federal Money Defends It
hook: Thousands of county and city offices actually run American elections — but the cyber defense behind them leans on federal money and expertise. When that support pauses, the vulnerability is local.

title: A Reform Gets Promised. Then What?
hook: DHS promised body cameras for every immigration agent after a fatal shooting. Six months later, two more people are dead — and still no cameras.

title: Why an Agency Is Harder to Abolish Than to Announce
hook: A president can reshape an agency's leadership and priorities quickly. Erasing it is a different act, because the agency exists in statute and its money is appropriated by Congress.

title: Major Political Ideologies
hook: An ideology is a worldview about how society should be run — and a handful of them frame most political arguments you'll ever hear.

title: When Organizing Beats Spending
hook: Money buys attention, not turnout. A Florida Senate primary won by the massively outspent candidate is a reminder of what a volunteer ground game can still do.

title: Why the Out-Party Runs on Corruption
hook: Democrats mentioned corruption six times as often in 2026 constituent emails as in 2022. That jump says less about new scandals than about what corruption does for a party with no power to legislate.

title: The Reform Almost Nobody Can Name
hook: About 2% of those polled could name proportional representation unprompted. Told what it does, half backed it — opinion on institutions stays latent until someone describes them.

title: The Eighth Amendment & Methods of Execution
hook: The Constitution bars 'cruel and unusual' punishment — so courts must decide not only whether a state may execute, but whether the method it chooses is constitutional.

title: Censure: Punishment Without Removal
hook: Legislatures mostly cannot fire their own members easily — voters hired them. So they built a middle sanction: a formal, recorded statement that the chamber disapproves.

title: Who Gets to Set the Size of the Court
hook: Nine justices feels constitutional. It is not — the number is ordinary law, which is exactly why proposals to freeze it at nine keep appearing.

title: The Hearing Before the Job: How Senate Confirmation Works
hook: Cabinet secretaries don't just get appointed — the Senate gets a vote first. A contentious July 2026 hearing for the next attorney general shows the confirmation gauntlet at work.

title: Taxation & Public Budgets
hook: A government's budget is its values written in numbers — and taxation is how it raises the money to act at all. Follow the money to understand the priorities.

title: The Distinction That Could Reshape Super PACs
hook: Citizens United protects unlimited independent spending. Maine's law doesn't touch spending — it caps what one donor may give the committee doing the spending. That gap is now in court.

title: When a Governor Pauses an Entire Industry by Executive Order
hook: Data-center fights used to be decided lot by lot, in local zoning meetings. In 2026 a governor skipped that entirely and paused the whole industry statewide.

title: Who Actually Sets the Rules for a Federal Election
hook: The Constitution hands the times, places and manner of congressional elections to state legislatures, with Congress able to override. The president is not on that list.

title: The Stopgap: Governing by Deadline
hook: Legislatures are supposed to pass budgets. When they cannot agree, many just extend last year's spending a few months at a time — and the deadline becomes the real negotiation.

title: When a Precedent Loses Its Foundation
hook: A 1980 ruling barred the Ten Commandments from public classrooms. An appeals court says the test it rested on is gone — so the ruling is too. That claim is now at the Supreme Court.

title: Globalization
hook: The world's economies have woven together so tightly that a decision in one country ripples through all the others — that deepening interdependence is globalization.

title: Diplomacy & War
hook: States pursue their interests on a spectrum that runs from the conference table to the battlefield. Diplomacy and war are two ends of the same toolkit.

title: What Government Is For
hook: Every society needs a way to make and enforce collective decisions — that shared system of authority is what we call government.

title: The $533 Million Factory That Made Nothing
hook: Government pays for defense capacity as it is built, not after it works. When the plant never produces, the taxpayer has already footed the bill.

title: Civil Liberties vs Civil Rights
hook: Two terms people mix up: liberties are freedoms from government interference; rights are protections to be treated equally.

title: Transgender Athletes & Equal Protection
hook: Can a state law treat male and female athletes differently and still satisfy the Constitution's promise of equal treatment? In 2026 the Supreme Court said yes, for school sports.

title: Why Noncitizen Voting Cases Are Hard to Prosecute
hook: A rule can be clear and the enforcement still collapse. Charging noncitizens with voting means proving they knew they were ineligible — and that is where the cases fall apart.

title: How Parades and Festivals Redefine 'One of Us'
hook: A Lunar New Year 5K, a Fourth of July parade with a woman in a sari, a festival that reclaims a slur — public celebrations quietly redraw who counts as a full member of the community.

title: Why Almost No Lawmakers Come From Working-Class Jobs
hook: Working-class people are about half the US labor force and about 1% of its lawmakers. The bottleneck isn't voters — it's who ever gets to run.

title: How Far Does One Judge's Order Reach?
hook: A court can block a policy for the people who sued — or for everyone, everywhere. The scope of an injunction can matter as much as who won.

title: The Rule of Law
hook: The principle that everyone — including those in power — is bound by the same publicly known laws, applied equally.

title: Immigration & Naturalization
hook: Every state has to answer two charged questions: who gets to come in, and who gets to become one of us? That's the politics of immigration and citizenship.

title: Who Are the "Friends of the Court"?
hook: Most briefs a supreme court reads are filed by people who aren't suing anyone. The amicus brief is how outside interests get a say in a case they are not party to.

title: Who Really Controls Grant Money
hook: The legislature appropriates the money, but the executive writes the rules for handing it out. A proposed U.S. rule would let officials end a federal grant 'at any time, for any reason.'

title: Why a Handful of Members Can Stall a Whole Agenda
hook: In a legislature with a thin majority, a bloc of a dozen members who vote together holds a veto — which is why intra-party factions often matter more than the other party does.

title: Why America Sorts Itself
hook: Red places get redder and blue places get bluer. Is it because people move to match their politics — or is politics just one reason among many?

title: Media & Conspiracy Belief
hook: Does what you watch shape what you believe? Researchers report that viewing one partisan cable outlet is associated with greater belief in a debunked conspiracy idea.

title: Deliberation Is a Skill, and It Can Be Designed
hook: Most public meetings are a queue of three-minute speeches at a panel. Deliberative democracy treats talking well as a designed process — with guides, trained facilitators, and no winner declared.

title: Refugees & Asylum
hook: When your own government becomes the threat, your last protection is the right to flee and seek safety elsewhere — the principle at the heart of refugee law.

title: Who Actually Pays to Run an Election
hook: National elections are run by local governments on local budgets. The people closest to the ballots are usually the ones worrying about affording them.

title: What a Chief Justice Actually Controls
hook: The chief justice's vote counts the same as everyone else's. The real power is procedural — who speaks, who writes, and in what order — and none of it is in the Constitution.

title: When Speed of Access to Official Speech Is for Sale
hook: A leader's posts move markets and policy. What happens to equal access when a company charges customers to receive them milliseconds sooner?

title: Devolution & Confederation
hook: Between a single central government and a loose alliance of states lies a spectrum — and where power sits on it shapes who can really decide.

title: Congress Holds the Court's Purse Strings, Too
hook: The judiciary doesn't get to set its own budget. In July 2026, Justices Kagan and Barrett had to go to Capitol Hill and ask for one — like any other federal agency.

title: How the Supreme Court Decides a Case
hook: A top court hears only a sliver of the cases that beg for its attention — and the path from petition to ruling runs through written briefs, a public argument, and a vote taken in secret.

title: Beyond the Swing Justice
hook: The 'swing vote' is a lazy model of a nine-member court. Sort four terms of close cases and you get two distinct jobs: building narrow majorities, and bridging the dissents nobody won.

title: Due Process
hook: Due process is the promise that the state can't take your liberty or property on a whim — it must follow fair, known rules before it acts against you.

title: The Left–Right Spectrum
hook: "Left" and "right" are political shorthand the whole world uses — but they began as nothing more than which side of a room people sat on.

title: Statute Law vs Common Law
hook: Not all law is written by legislators. Some of it is built up, case by case, by judges — and these two sources of law work very differently.

title: From Local Investigation to Federal Policy, in Two Months
hook: A local newsroom's investigation found California let dozens of teachers accused of sexual misconduct keep working. The federal government cited it directly when it acted.

title: A President Can Let a Bill Become Law by Doing Nothing
hook: Signing isn't the only way a bill becomes law — sometimes doing nothing at all has the exact same effect.

title: Dealignment, Not Realignment
hook: Working-class voters have been about a third of the American electorate for seventy years. What changed is not their size but their attachment — they left one party without joining the other.

title: The Law That Keeps Living Faces Off Money
hook: A new $1 coin puts a sitting president's face on U.S. currency for only the second time ever. Legal experts say the law was written to prevent exactly that.

title: Scientific Integrity Policies Are Only Words Until Tested
hook: Agencies that produce official numbers usually have a written rule barring political interference. It is an internal policy — which means the same agency can edit it.

title: Terrorism
hook: Terrorism is violence aimed less at its victims than at an audience — using fear as a political weapon to force change a group cannot win by other means.

title: Montesquieu's Other Warning: The Tyranny of Opinion
hook: Montesquieu is famous for separation of powers. His lesser-known warning: a constitution can be free on paper and still fail, once enough people stop believing its limits apply to them.

title: Referendums & Direct Democracy
hook: Usually we elect others to decide for us. Sometimes the people decide a question themselves — that's direct democracy, and the referendum is its main modern tool.

title: Racial Vote Dilution: When District Lines Split a Community
hook: Redrawing a map can quietly weaken a racial group's vote — split one community across enough districts and it may elect no one, even where its numbers are large.

title: Can the Government Force a Reporter to Reveal a Source?
hook: There's no absolute First Amendment shield protecting a journalist's sources — which is exactly what makes a federal subpoena for reporters' grand jury testimony such a live threat to the free press.

title: Why Parties Write Governing Plans Before They Win
hook: Long before an election, the out-of-power side is often already drafting exactly what it would do if it won — a governing blueprint built to be ready on day one.

title: Why Vote Counts Shift After Election Night
hook: Watch a close race and the leader can flip in the days after polls close. The usual cause is boring — who votes by mail, and when those ballots get counted — not fraud.

title: The Cap on What Judges Can Earn on the Side
hook: Federal judges may only earn a few tens of thousands of dollars outside the job — a rule meant to keep outside money from buying influence. Writing books is one of the carve-outs.

title: Regulatory Capture
hook: Who protects a city's drinking water when the industry that put it at risk is also the one the regulator was built to serve? That's the problem political scientists call regulatory capture.

title: Reading a Justice by the Numbers
hook: Label a judge 'conservative' and you've explained almost nothing. Code 311 of Barrett's decisions and a sharper pattern appears: she asks whether a ruling reaches further than the authority behind it.

title: When Detention Is a Revenue Line
hook: Contract out a coercive government function and you create a company whose earnings rise with enforcement — and whose shareholders now have a stake in how the policy goes.

title: Why It's So Hard to Sue Your Health Insurer
hook: A 1974 law meant to protect pensions also quietly shields most employer health plans from lawsuits over wrongly denied claims — even when the denial causes real harm.

title: Terrorism Charges Without an Ideology
hook: Texas is prosecuting a teenage shooting spree as terrorism with no manifesto and no extremist ties — testing whether the crime is defined by motive or by the fear it creates.

title: Protected by a Rule, Not by a Law
hook: Whatever one administration can create with a regulation, the next can undo with a regulation. The move to reopen roadless national forests to logging shows how thin that kind of protection is.

title: Why Outsiders Keep Capturing 'Establishment' Parties
hook: Modern parties look powerful on television and weak up close — most have little real control over who runs under their banner. That gap is what lets outsider candidates walk in and take over.

title: Why Bail Is Rare in Extradition Cases
hook: Bail turns on one question: will this person come back? Extradition cases are the setting where courts trust that answer least.

title: A Voting Rule Needs a System Behind It
hook: Writing a new election rule is the easy part. Building the machinery that can execute it before the next election is where rules quietly turn into disenfranchisement.

title: Theories of International Relations
hook: Why do states behave as they do? Three big theories give rival answers — and which lens you use changes what you see in every global event.

title: The Great Lakes Program Both Parties Keep Funding
hook: Since 2010 the U.S. has spent over $5 billion cleaning up the Great Lakes — and it has survived Congress after Congress. The coalition behind it is a case study in building bipartisan support.

title: How Redefining One Word Can Rewrite a Law
hook: Congress didn't touch the Endangered Species Act. An agency just redefined what "habitat" means — and, critics say, quietly stripped out one of its main protections.

title: There's No 25th Amendment for Congress
hook: When a president is incapacitated, the Constitution has a formal fix: the 25th Amendment. When a senator is hospitalized for weeks with no details given, there isn't one.

title: Precautionary Diplomacy
hook: Most treaties clean up a mess after it happens. A rarer kind acts first — banning commercial fishing in the Arctic before it even begins, to buy time for science.

title: The 60-Day Clock That Keeps Getting Reset
hook: The War Powers Resolution gives Congress 60 days to approve a war before the president must stop — but a new 'notice' can restart the clock, and Congress has struggled to make its objection stick.

title: How a Federal Agency Changes Its Own Rules — No New Law Required
hook: After a string of deadly shootings tied to its officers, ICE didn't wait for Congress to act. It just changed its own internal policy — a reminder of how much agencies can do on their own.

title: The Politics of Climate Change
hook: Climate change is a global commons problem at the largest scale — which is exactly why it's so politically hard: the costs are now, local, and certain; the benefits, future and shared.

title: Rulemaking Is Supposed to Include the Public — What Happens When It Doesn't
hook: Before a federal agency can change a regulation, it's normally required to ask the public first. A 2026 overhaul of grazing rules on federal land tested how easily that step can be trimmed.

title: Technology & Democracy
hook: The internet promised to supercharge democracy — more voice, more information, more connection. It delivered that, and a tangle of new threats alongside it.

title: Even a Superpower Can't Just Order a Sovereign Country to Comply
hook: The U.S. indicted Mexican officials on drug-corruption charges and threatened economic penalties. Mexico's president said no anyway — a case study in the real limits of sovereignty.

title: Is Calling Something 'The Big Lie' an Opinion?
hook: Defamation law protects opinion but not false facts — so the whole fight is over which side of that line a phrase falls on. Trump's suit against CNN asks the Supreme Court to redraw it.

title: Strings Attached: When Federal Money Becomes Leverage
hook: A national government that can't order regions around directly can often get the same result by attaching conditions to its money — which is why courts ask where persuasion ends and coercion begins.

title: Unitary vs Federal Systems
hook: Where does the final say live — with one national government, or shared with regions? That choice shapes how a country is run.

title: The Senate Parliamentarian
hook: The Senate's nonpartisan rules referee — an unelected adviser who can quietly reshape major bills by ruling on what the chamber's own procedures allow.

title: The Constitution Has Clauses Courts Won't Touch
hook: Not every line in the Constitution gets fought over in court. Some, like the ban on quartering soldiers, have sat almost untouched for over two centuries — by choice, not by accident.

title: The Memo Congress Never Voted On
hook: A presidential memorandum can direct 200-plus FBI task forces to hunt down a whole ideology — no bill, no vote, and no requirement it even be made public.

title: Regulating Nuclear Power: Speed vs. Safety
hook: Speeding up approval for new nuclear reactors could mean cheaper, faster clean power — or it could mean cutting the safety review that catches problems first. Regulators have to choose.

title: The Discount Airtime Rule — and Who Counts as a Candidate
hook: U.S. law forces broadcasters to sell candidates ad time at their lowest rate near an election. The 2026 fight is not over the discount, but over who gets to claim it.

title: Air Force One and the Modern Presidency
hook: A historian's argument that the presidency we recognize today — constantly travelling, personally diplomatic, permanently campaigning — was built by an airplane.

title: Do People Trust the Court, or Just Their Side of It?
hook: Only 46% of Americans approve of the Supreme Court overall — but break it down by party, and the real story is a 56-point gap in how Republicans and Democrats see the same institution.

title: The Newspaper Editorial Is Disappearing
hook: Pulitzer editorial entries fell from 101 in 1995 to 25 this year, as chains swapped local editorials for syndicated columns — leaving a hole in local accountability.

title: FISA Section 702
hook: The law behind much of America's foreign-intelligence collection — powerful enough to feed most of the president's daily brief, yet it expires unless Congress keeps renewing it.

title: The Internet Subsidy Program Paying to Wire Empty Buildings
hook: Phone customers nationwide pay over $340,000 a year to keep a nearly-abandoned Alaska island 'wired' for slow internet — while the few people who actually live there just use Starlink.

title: The Study Its Own University Asked to Have Retracted
hook: A university audit found a celebrated study had no ethics approval and unverifiable data. Three years later the journal answered with a 78-word correction — and the study kept guiding care.

title: When a Gun-Permit Decision Becomes a Federal Civil Rights Case
hook: A city police department can revoke a concealed-carry license for 'good cause.' Who that standard gets applied to is what can turn it into a federal civil rights investigation.

title: The Beating That Asked: Is Some Speech Itself Violence?
hook: In 1856, a congressman beat a senator unconscious with a cane over an anti-slavery speech — and forced America to argue over whether words can be treated as an act of violence.

title: What the Election Assistance Commission Does — and Why Its Independence Matters
hook: A little-known federal commission certifies voting machines and helps run U.S. elections. In 2026 the president removed its last sitting members, months before the midterms.

title: Sanctions: The Weapon States Reach For Before They Reach For Weapons
hook: Cutting a country off from money and markets sits between a strongly-worded letter and a war — which is exactly why governments use it so often, and why it so often disappoints.

title: Tribal Water Rights & Interstate Compacts
hook: Seven states share the Colorado River under a 100-year-old compact that barely mentions the tribes with some of the oldest legal claims to its water. Updating that deal is proving hard.

title: The Exemption That Hides a Billion Dollars
hook: Oregon publishes what it spends on affordable housing. What it won't publish is what the money bought — an exemption written into its records law in 1997, and almost nobody voted against it.

title: Why Outside Money Loves a Primary
hook: A dollar spent in a low-turnout primary buys far more influence than the same dollar in a general election — which is where super PACs increasingly aim it.

title: Gifts, Regulators, and the Companies They Regulate
hook: Two FCC officials took pricey gala tickets from Paramount while the company had billions of dollars in mergers awaiting the agency's approval. Ethics rules exist for exactly this.

title: When a Private School Is 100% Publicly Funded
hook: Some private schools get every dollar of their tuition from taxpayers — yet the conflict-of-interest, open-records, and open-meeting rules that come with public money don't follow it in.

title: What Public Policy Is
hook: Passing a law is just the start. Public policy is the whole arc — from defining a problem to actually delivering a solution and seeing whether it worked.

title: The Director of National Intelligence
hook: After 9/11, the U.S. created one job to make its spy agencies talk to each other — and a veteran argues the role needs expertise, not just political loyalty.

title: Declassified Isn't the Same as New
hook: A primetime address, declassified documents, and warnings of 'shocking vulnerabilities' in U.S. elections — but reviewers found the documents mostly repeated what officials already knew years ago.

title: Consent Decrees & Police Oversight
hook: When a police department is found to systematically violate rights, the usual fix is a federal consent decree — a court-enforced reform plan. What happens when the enforcer stops enforcing?

title: Consent Is the Biggest Exception
hook: A warrantless search of a home is presumptively unreasonable — unless you say yes. And nobody is required to tell you that you may say no.

title: Key Political Thinkers
hook: A handful of thinkers, writing across two millennia, still frame the questions we argue about: who should rule, why obey, and how to stop power going bad?

title: When the State Contracts Out Custody, Oversight Doesn't Follow
hook: Governments can delegate the job of locking someone up. What often fails to travel with the contract is the duty to open the records.

title: How Votes Become Seats
hook: The same ballots can produce very different results depending on the electoral system used to count them.

title: The Supreme Court of Israel
hook: A court that built constitutional review out of ordinary statutes, opened its doors to almost any petitioner — and is now, for the first time, itself the central issue in a national election.

title: What Human Rights Are
hook: Human rights are the radical claim that every person — regardless of country, status, or who's in charge — holds certain basic rights simply by being human.

title: Why Tariff Fights Escalate
hook: The U.S. put 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian goods; Canada said within hours it would hit back. That reflex — retaliate, don't absorb — is what turns a tariff into a trade war.

title: The Supreme Court's 'Shadow Docket'
hook: Most Supreme Court rulings today aren't fully-argued opinions — they're fast, often unsigned orders with little explanation. In the term ending October 2025, those quietly became the majority.

title: Enforcing Human Rights
hook: Declaring a right is easy; enforcing it against a sovereign state is hard. The global human-rights system relies more on pressure and exposure than on a world police.

title: The UN & International Organizations
hook: Sovereign states that answer to no one above them still build standing clubs to cooperate. The UN is the largest — a forum, not a world government.

title: The Supreme Court's Other Docket
hook: The Court hears about sixty argued cases a year and disposes of thousands more by short written order. Most of what it does never gets an opinion at all.

title: The Ancient Origins of Politics
hook: The words we still use — politics, democracy, republic — were coined in ancient Greece and Rome, where the first experiments in self-rule were run.

title: The Free Press & Democracy
hook: A free press is sometimes called the "fourth estate" — an unofficial branch of power whose job is to watch the other three on the public's behalf.

title: The One-Justice Order That Freezes a Case
hook: Before the Supreme Court decides anything, a single justice can push pause. That's how White House ballroom construction kept going after two lower courts had ordered it stopped.

title: State Constitutions Can Guarantee More Than the Federal One Does
hook: The U.S. Constitution sets a floor of rights, not a ceiling. New York's constitution goes further — it makes aiding the needy a state duty, not just a policy choice.

title: Why No Cameras in the Supreme Court?
hook: You can read every Supreme Court ruling, but you can't watch the arguments on video. The long fight over courtroom cameras is really a fight over judicial transparency.

title: The 'Tenth Justice': Government's Lawyer at the Court
hook: One lawyer appears in most Supreme Court cases, keeps an office inside the courthouse, and shapes what the Court decides by choosing which questions to put in front of it.

title: Environmental Governance
hook: How do you regulate something that ignores borders and belongs to no one? Environmental governance is the toolkit societies use to manage nature collectively.

title: Did Troops Cut D.C. Crime?
hook: A new study found the National Guard's deployment in Washington, D.C. had no measurable effect on violent crime — a case study in evaluating public-safety policy with evidence.

title: Prediction Markets in Politics
hook: Let people bet real money on who wins, and the prices start to look like odds — a crowd-sourced forecast. But betting on politics invites its own kind of trouble.

title: The Housing Policy That Sits Between a Shelter and a Home
hook: Building apartments takes years. Emergency shelters help for a night. Tiny house villages spread because they fit the gap — and because local rules allow them faster.

title: The Poll Behind the Headlines: More Agreement Than It Looks
hook: Ask Americans about the country's 250th anniversary and you get a partisan split. Ask about the country's founding ideals and something odd happens: the numbers converge.

title: Why Texas Dominates the Supreme Court's Docket
hook: Of the 35 cases with individual litigants the Supreme Court heard this term, five centered on Texans — more than double any other state. It's not Texas law that's unusual; it's the plumbing above it.

title: Disinformation & Propaganda
hook: Democracy depends on citizens being informed — so deliberately polluting what they know is a direct attack on it. That's the threat of propaganda and disinformation.

title: The Hunger Strike, and What Outlives It
hook: A 26-day fast in India drew a national audience and helped ignite a youth movement — then the fast ended and the protests didn't, which is the more telling part.

title: Why Primary Polls Are the Hardest Polls
hook: General-election polling has a stable anchor: party. Primaries strip that anchor away, which is why the same pollsters who do fine in November can miss badly in a primary.

title: What Happens After a Court Voids a Tax
hook: Courts can strike down a tax — but the money is already collected and spent. The unwinding of one tariff program has reached about $100 billion in refunds, and it is far from finished.

title: Firing an Official Can Require a Hearing First
hook: The fight over removing a Federal Reserve governor turned on something narrower than presidential power: whether she gets told the charge and a chance to answer before she is out.

title: Maps as Political Power
hook: A map looks like neutral fact, but someone chose what to show, what to leave out, and where to draw the line — and those choices shape voting, travel, and spending.

title: How You Put a Number on Human Rights
hook: Rights either exist or they don't — so how does anyone score a country? Researchers do it by reading the reports, coding the incidents, and correcting for a nasty bias.

title: The Right to Bear Arms
hook: How does a court decide which weapons are protected? The U.S. Supreme Court's answer turns on a deceptively simple phrase: arms 'in common use.'

title: Why Moving Children Is a War Crime
hook: International law singles out the transfer of children in wartime for special protection — because taking a child across a border can erase an identity that no ceasefire will restore.

title: Markets, Regulation & the Mixed Economy
hook: Pure free market or full state control? Almost every country picks neither — they run a mixed economy, and where they draw the line is one of politics' great arguments.

title: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
hook: After a world war and the Holocaust, nations did something unprecedented: they wrote down, together, a common list of rights belonging to everyone on Earth.

title: Voting Rights & the Map Fight
hook: The Supreme Court let Alabama use a congressional map a lower court called racially discriminatory — a window into the Voting Rights Act and how redistricting fights reach the Court.

title: Public Money, Private Oversight: The Voucher Accountability Gap
hook: Public schools face extensive state regulation. Private schools funded by the same taxpayer dollars, through vouchers, often don't — a gap one Arkansas case exposed starkly.

title: When a Flood Buyout Can't Reach the People Who Flooded
hook: Disaster buyouts retire dangerous land by purchasing homes. If the residents rent a lot and own a trailer classified as personal property, there is often nothing for the program to buy.

title: The Constitutional Court of South Africa
hook: Born out of the end of apartheid, this court was designed to make a new constitution stick — and became one of the world's most-cited voices on what rights a government owes its people.

title: Tribal Nations as a Third Sovereign
hook: American federalism is usually taught as states versus Washington. That leaves out hundreds of tribal governments whose authority predates the Constitution itself.

title: What Counts as Voter ID
hook: A voter ID law is really two decisions: require an ID, then decide which IDs count. The second one quietly determines who gets turned away.

title: Surveillance & Privacy
hook: Technology lets states and companies watch people at a scale once unimaginable — putting the old right to be left alone on a collision course with security and profit.

title: When Locking People Up Is the Local Jobs Plan
hook: Rural places have sold prison beds to distant governments since the 1800s. Immigration detention has revived the trade — and with it an economy that grows only when enforcement does.

title: A Law 'Trapped in Amber'
hook: One throwaway metaphor from a Supreme Court opinion is now everywhere in the lower courts — and scholars disagree about whether it smuggles in a whole theory of the constitution.

title: Treaties & International Law
hook: If no world government can pass laws, how do nations bind themselves at all? Largely by agreeing to — treaties are the contracts that knit the international order together.

title: Mission Creep: When a Body Outgrows Its Stated Job
hook: Memphis got a federal task force announced to fight violent crime. Ten months on, it had driven a surge of immigration arrests — mostly of people with no convictions. A study in how missions drift.

title: Party Spending & Campaign Finance
hook: Since Watergate, a law has capped how much a political party can spend directly coordinating with its own candidate. In 2026 the Supreme Court struck that cap down.

title: Dangerous, But Not Dangerous Enough to Fix
hook: Omaha yards can hold enough lead to harm a child and still fail to qualify for cleanup — because the rule that decides who gets help was written to a 1994 understanding of the risk.

title: What Primary Results Can't Tell You
hook: Every primary night produces a verdict on where a party is headed. The results themselves rarely support one — a handful of low-turnout races is a noisy signal about ideology.

title: What a Constitution Is
hook: The rulebook above the rules: a constitution sets out how a government is structured and the limits on its power.

title: A Time Limit Only Binds If Someone Counts the Clock
hook: A 72-hour cap on holding someone sounds like a hard limit. It is only as hard as the rule about when the count starts over.

title: A Court Can Order Treatment. It Can't Order the Appointment to Exist.
hook: A county can now court-order outpatient mental health treatment — but of 279 Medicaid providers listed, a study found only 34 had open appointments. Legal authority alone doesn't deliver a service.

title: A Law Can Take Effect Before Courts Decide If It's Legal
hook: Texas requires parental permission before minors can download most apps. Courts haven't ruled it constitutional — but the Supreme Court's emergency docket let it take effect anyway.

title: Can AI Verify a Signature on a Ballot? Experts Say Not Yet
hook: The FBI explored using AI to check signatures on seized mail-in ballots — a case study in what happens when new technology meets an old, imperfect forensic method.

title: Deregulation Without Repealing Anything
hook: You do not need to repeal a consumer protection law to switch it off. Stop investigating, ask companies nicely, and take their word for it — the statute stays on the books, unenforced.

title: Junk Science & Wrongful Conviction
hook: A courtroom isn't a lab — but it has to rely on forensic science anyway. When that science turns out to be unreliable, the wrong person can spend years, or a life, on death row.

title: The Judiciary & Judicial Review
hook: Courts don't just settle disputes between people — through judicial review, many can also strike down a law or an official act that violates the constitution.

title: Political Legitimacy
hook: Power can rest on fear alone, but it lasts when people believe it is rightful. That belief — legitimacy — is what separates authority from mere force.

title: Who Commands the National Guard?
hook: The National Guard answers to two masters at once — a state governor and the president. A 2026 stand-off over troops in D.C. shows what happens when they pull in different directions.

title: "Clearly Established" Law and Qualified Immunity
hook: A right you hold on paper can be unenforceable in court: officials escape damages unless a prior ruling already said, in nearly identical facts, that what they did was illegal.

title: The Side Door Into a Closed Facility
hook: Journalists can't get inside an immigration detention camp. But when the camp dials 911, the call lands in a county system — where public records law still applies.

title: The Enlightenment & Modern Politics
hook: The radical idea that legitimate power comes from the people — not God or birth — was forged in the Enlightenment, and it still underpins democracy today.

title: What a Concurrence Is For
hook: A concurring justice agrees with the outcome — and sometimes uses the space to propose demolishing the doctrine the majority just applied. Today's lone concurrence is tomorrow's majority.

title: The Power of a Dissent
hook: A dissenting judge loses the case — but a sharp dissent can outlive the majority, persuading future courts or pushing lawmakers to rewrite the rule.

title: The European Court of Justice
hook: A court above nations: it doesn't replace any country's supreme court, but it makes sure EU law means the same thing in every member state.

title: Trust Is a Behavior, Not a Credential
hook: Credentials tell you who is qualified. They do not tell anyone whether to act on your advice — and acting on advice, at some risk to yourself, is what trust actually is.

title: What 'Insolvency' Actually Means for a Trust Fund
hook: Most Americans think the Social Security trust fund running out means no checks. It means smaller checks — and the gap between those two beliefs is why the fix keeps getting deferred.

title: Democratic Backsliding
hook: Democracies rarely die in a single coup anymore. More often they erode — legally, gradually, step by step — until little is left but the shell of elections.

title: Local Government
hook: The layer of government you meet most often isn't the national one — it's the city or council that runs your streets, schools, and rubbish collection.

title: A Speedy Remedy That Isn't Speedy
hook: Habeas corpus lets a detained person ask a judge one question: is this lawful? The protection depends on getting an answer quickly — and ProPublica found some judges take months.

title: Freedom of Expression
hook: The freedom to speak, publish, and dissent is often called the first freedom — because without it, citizens can't check power or argue their way to better decisions.

title: Why Living Leaders Almost Never Appear on Money — Unless They're Royalty
hook: A count of nearly 1,000 world coins found sitting leaders appear almost exclusively in hereditary monarchies — which is why putting an elected president on currency reads as a monarchical move.

title: Losing in Court Isn't Always the End of a Policy
hook: A court judgment binds the order in front of it. Rewrite the order and the clock restarts at the bottom of the judicial ladder — sometimes for years.

title: Whose Park Is It, Anyway?
hook: Lafayette Square has hosted protests aimed at the White House for generations. A proposal for a permanent 8-to-9-foot fence around it puts security and free assembly on a literal collision course.

title: How Precedent Erodes
hook: Courts rarely kill an old ruling outright. More often it dies slowly — narrowed, distinguished, and ignored until little is left.

title: Giving a Country Weapons vs. Teaching It to Build Them
hook: Shipping missiles buys a partner time. Sharing the blueprints changes what it can do without you — which is why technology transfer is a bigger decision than any single delivery.

title: When Federal Law Overrides the States
hook: Who decides what warning goes on a bottle of weed killer — a state jury or the federal government? The answer turns on a quiet but powerful rule called preemption.

title: Exonerated Isn't the Same as Compensated
hook: Getting a conviction thrown out does not get you paid. In most states you must then prove your innocence all over again — to a higher standard, against a state that may still call you guilty.

title: Not All Dissents Are Created Equal
hook: Dissent tallies treat a one-line 'I would deny' the same as a fully reasoned opinion. One scholar sorted 386 of them on the emergency docket — and found about half were just bare votes.

title: The Appeal After the Last Appeal
hook: When the Supreme Court declines your case, one option remains: ask it to reconsider. It has not granted such a request since 2018.

title: Voter Turnout & Engagement
hook: Who shows up changes who wins. Turnout — the share of eligible people who actually vote — is one of the quiet forces shaping every election.

title: The Provisional Ballot: Vote First, Sort It Out Later
hook: The worst way to resolve an eligibility dispute is at the check-in table while the line grows. The provisional ballot exists so you can vote now and let officials verify afterward.

title: You Don't Have to Live in the District You Represent
hook: The Constitution asks a House candidate to be an inhabitant of the state — not the district. That gap is why 'carpetbagger' is an insult and not a disqualification.

title: Soft Power & Hard Power
hook: States get their way two ways: by force and money, or by attraction. Knowing the difference between hard power and soft power explains a lot about how influence really works.

title: Temporary Protected Status
hook: Some immigrants are allowed to stay not because they won asylum, but because their home country is too dangerous to return to — for now. That 'for now' is the whole idea.

title: Who Decides What to Charge
hook: A prosecutor builds a case; headquarters picks the charge. That chain of command is normal — and it is also the point where a case can be quietly downgraded.

title: The Civil Service & Bureaucracy
hook: Governments change; the bureaucracy stays. The permanent civil service is the machinery that actually delivers policy — for better and, sometimes, for worse.

title: Global Inequality & Development
hook: Where you're born still shapes your life chances more than almost anything else. Closing that gap between rich and poor nations is one of politics' great unfinished projects.

title: Who Decides Which State Votes First?
hook: The order states vote in a presidential nominating contest isn't set by any constitution — it's a party rule, and parties rewrite it to change whose voters get courted first.

title: Birthright Citizenship & the 14th Amendment
hook: Born on U.S. soil, you're a citizen — full stop, according to the Constitution's plain text. In 2026 the Supreme Court reaffirmed that even a presidential order can't rewrite it.

title: Social Movements & Protest
hook: When ordinary channels fail or move too slowly, people organize and take to the streets. Social movements are how the unrepresented push change onto the agenda.

title: Where a 'Right to Privacy' Comes From
hook: The word 'privacy' never appears in the U.S. Constitution. Decades of doctrine hang on where courts decided to find it — and a long-running argument says they looked in the wrong place.

title: Zoning as a Housing Policy Lever: the "Missing Middle"
hook: Nearly 70% of Denver's residential land allows only single-family houses. A simulator estimates that letting four units build anywhere would raise market-rate multifamily supply 46%.

title: Why Census Data Has 'Noise' Added
hook: To stop anyone reverse-engineering your identity from public statistics, the U.S. census deliberately blurs its own numbers — a privacy-for-accuracy trade with real political stakes.

title: How Lawmakers Fund Each Other
hook: Some of the most important campaign money in Congress doesn't come from voters or donors — it flows between lawmakers themselves, and it quietly buys power.

title: Abortion After Dobbs
hook: In 2022 the Supreme Court did something rare: it withdrew a constitutional right it had recognized for half a century — and handed the question back to the states.

title: What an Executive Order Can and Cannot Change
hook: A presidential order can tell the executive branch what to aim for. It can't skip the process an agency must follow — which is why headlines and reality often diverge.

title: Who Checks Whether a Cleanup Held?
hook: The EPA remediated 13,000 Omaha yards and moved on. Reporters retested 620 of them for $10 a sample — and found lead above the agency's own trigger in four of every ten.
